newsitem.title: POLAND: FOCUS - Zloty devaluation rate to lag expected CPI.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Zloty devaluation rate to lag expected CPI.

text.p: The National Bank of Poland (NBP) will maintain the crawling peg devaluation of the zloty next year and will keep its devaluation rate below that of expected inflation, the bank said in a statement on Friday.

"The NBP informs that next year the mechanism of the crawling devaluation of the zloty central parity rate will be maintained, while the monthly pace of this devaluation will be kept at a lower level than expected inflation," it said.

In a report on Thursday, Reuters incorrectly quoted NBP President Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz as saying the central bank should slow the monthly devaluation rate from the current one percent after year-on-year inflation falls to 13 percent.
Gronkiewicz-Waltz in fact said that, as Poland aimed to slash inflation to the 13 percent target in December next year, the rate of the zloty devaluation would have to be reduced to help the process.
"I think that we have to reduce inflation to 13 percent, so because of this the crawling peg should be reduced, not so much, but should be reduced," she told Reuters on Thursday.
Friday's central bank statement made clear that the 13 percent level -- next year's government inflation target -- was not a precondition for slowing the zloty devaluation.
The year-on-year inflation was at 19.5 percent in September, down from 21.6 percent in 1995.

Analysts see the 13 percent in 1997 as an ambitious goal as Poland would likely miss its 1996 target of 17 percent inflation under pressure from fast rising food prices and high oil prices. The budget plan for 1996 originally assumed the average rate of the monthly zloty devaluation against a basket of western currencies at 0.9 percent monthly.
But the central bank has held the rate at one percent since it last cut it from 1.2 percent early in January.
Analysts have said further reductions in the devaluation rate would help reduce inflation but a resulting relative strengthening of the zloty could harm Poland's already deteriorating trade balance.

After the first eight months of this year Poland had a current account surplus of $48 million and a trade shortfall of $4.5 billion. The government forecasts that the trade deficit will widen to $9 billion next year.
